tips.title: Dashed is the open circle
tips.body: On a number line a strict inequality gets an **open circle**; on a graph it gets a **dashed line**. Same idea, same mark. $\leqslant$ and $\geqslant$ get a **solid** line, and points on it count.

tips.title: Test (0, 0) rather than reasoning
tips.body: To decide which side to shade, substitute $(0, 0)$ into the inequality. If it works, shade the side with the origin. It needs no rearranging, so the symbol cannot flip on you — which is exactly how the side gets chosen wrongly.

tips.title: Substitute a point into every inequality
tips.body: Once shaded, take a point clearly inside and test it against **all** of them. If any fails, a side is shaded the wrong way. It takes seconds and it is the only way to catch a reversed region, which is otherwise invisible.

tips.title: The largest value sits at a corner
tips.body: Asked for the greatest value of something like $x + 2y$ inside a region, test the **corners** only. The expression changes steadily along each edge, so its extremes are at the ends — three or four substitutions, no searching.

steps.title: An inequality in two variables
steps.body:
This whole topic is **Higher tier**.

An inequality like $y > 2x - 1$ has two variables, so a single solution is a **pair** of numbers: a point $(x, y)$. There are infinitely many, and together they fill a **region** of the graph.

The method has three steps, and they are the same every time.

1. Draw the **boundary line**, treating the inequality as an equation. For $y > 2x - 1$, draw $y = 2x - 1$.
2. Make the line **dashed** if the inequality is strict ($<$ or $>$), or **solid** if it includes the line ($\leqslant$ or $\geqslant$).
3. Shade the side that satisfies it.

The dashed and solid convention is the two-variable version of the open and filled circles on a number line, and it carries a mark in exactly the same way.

steps.title: Which side to shade
steps.body:
Deciding the side is where most marks are lost, and there is a method that never fails: **test a point**.

Pick any point that is clearly not on the line — $(0, 0)$ is ideal when the line does not pass through the origin — and put it into the inequality. If it works, shade that side. If it does not, shade the other side.

That is more reliable than reasoning about which way the inequality points, because rearranging can flip things without your noticing.

steps.title: Several inequalities at once
steps.body:
A question usually gives **three or four** inequalities and asks for the region satisfying **all** of them. That region is the **overlap**.

Take $x \geqslant 0$, $y \geqslant 0$ and $x + y \leqslant 5$.

- $x \geqslant 0$ is everything to the **right** of the y axis, with a solid boundary.
- $y \geqslant 0$ is everything **above** the x axis, solid.
- $x + y \leqslant 5$ is everything **below** the line $x + y = 5$, solid.

The three together give a **triangle** with vertices at $(0,0)$, $(5,0)$ and $(0,5)$.

To draw $x + y = 5$ quickly, find where it crosses the axes: put $x = 0$ to get $y = 5$, and $y = 0$ to get $x = 5$. Join $(0,5)$ to $(5,0)$. That is far faster than making a table of values.

Label the region **R**, because the question will ask you to.

steps.title: Reading a region off a graph
steps.body:
The question also comes the other way round: a region is drawn, and you have to write down the inequalities.

Work through the boundaries one at a time.

1. Find the **equation of each boundary line**, using its gradient and intercept, or its axis crossings.
2. Decide the **symbol** from the line style: dashed means $<$ or $>$, solid means $\leqslant$ or $\geqslant$.
3. Decide the **direction** by testing a point **inside** the shaded region.

Step 3 is the one to be careful with. Pick a point that is clearly inside, substitute it, and see which way the inequality has to point for it to be true.

For the triangle above, a point inside is $(1, 1)$. Testing it: $1 \geqslant 0$ ✓, $1 \geqslant 0$ ✓, and $1 + 1 = 2 \leqslant 5$ ✓. All three hold, which confirms the three inequalities are right.

steps.title: Integer points inside a region
steps.body:
A common follow-up asks for the **integer coordinates** inside the region, or the point that makes something largest.

For the triangle $x \geqslant 0$, $y \geqslant 0$, $x + y \leqslant 5$, the integer points are those with whole-number coordinates satisfying all three. There are **21** of them.

Count them **systematically**, column by column, or you will miss some.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.** On one set of axes, shade the region satisfying all three of

$$x \geqslant 1, \qquad y > x, \qquad x + y \leqslant 6$$

1. Which boundaries are solid and which are dashed? Say why for each.
2. Draw and shade the region, and label it R.
3. Test the point $(2, 3)$. Is it in the region? Show your working for all three inequalities.

**Part B.**

4. Write down the coordinates of one integer point inside the region.
5. Is $(1, 1)$ inside it? Explain using one of the inequalities.

Question 5 is the one to think about: $(1, 1)$ satisfies two of the three.

check.prompt: Is the point $(1, 1)$ in the region $x \geqslant 1$, $y > x$, $x + y \leqslant 6$?
check.solution: $x \geqslant 1$ ✓ and $1 + 1 = 2 \leqslant 6$ ✓, but $y > x$ needs $1 > 1$, which is **false**. The point lies **on** the dashed boundary, and a dashed line is excluded.

steps.title: Going deeper: the boundary is where the marks are
steps.body:
Two things separate a full-mark answer here, and both concern the **boundary** rather than the shading.

**First: a point on a dashed line is not in the region.** This is the two-variable version of the open circle, and it is tested directly. $(1, 1)$ against $y > x$ gives $1 > 1$, which is false. The point sits exactly on the line, so it is out. Students who shade beautifully still lose this mark.

**Second: say what you shaded.** Some questions ask you to shade the region that satisfies the inequalities; others ask you to shade the region that does **not**, leaving the answer unshaded. Read which, and label **R** on the part you mean. An unlabelled diagram can be read either way, and the examiner will not guess in your favour.

**A check worth doing every time.** Once shaded, take a point clearly inside and substitute it into **all** the inequalities. If any fails, your shading is wrong somewhere. It takes a few seconds and it catches a reversed side, which is otherwise invisible.

**Where regions lead.** A question may ask which point in the region makes something largest — for instance the greatest value of $x + 2y$. The answer is always at a **corner** of the region, because moving along any edge changes the expression steadily, so the extreme is at an end. Testing the three or four corners is enough; you never need to test the interior.

That last idea is the beginning of linear programming, and knowing it turns a hard-looking question into arithmetic on three points.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- This topic is **Higher tier**.
- An inequality in two variables is satisfied by a **region** of points, not by single numbers.
- Draw the **boundary** by treating the inequality as an equation.
- **Dashed** for $<$ and $>$; **solid** for $\leqslant$ and $\geqslant$. This is the two-variable open and filled circle.
- Decide the side by **testing a point**, usually $(0, 0)$. It needs no rearranging, so nothing can flip.
- For several inequalities, the region is the **overlap** of all of them.
- Draw a line like $x + y = 5$ from its **axis crossings**: $(0, 5)$ and $(5, 0)$.
- Reading a region off a graph: equation from the line, symbol from the **line style**, direction from a **point inside**.
- A point **on a dashed line is not in the region**.
- Always **label R**, and read whether the question wants the region shaded or left unshaded.
- Count integer points **column by column**, so none is missed. The triangle here has **21**.
- The largest or smallest value of an expression in a region is always at a **corner**.

questions.prompt: Which point is inside the region $x \geqslant 1$, $y > x$, $x + y \leqslant 6$?
Shade the region satisfying $x \geqslant 1$, $y > x$ and $x + y \leqslant 6$. Say which boundaries are dashed and which are solid, and show that $(2, 3)$ lies inside the region.
questions.solution: The boundary of the first inequality is the vertical line x equals one, drawn solid because the symbol includes the line. The boundary of the second is the line y equals x, drawn dashed because the symbol is strictly greater than, so points on the line are not part of the region. The boundary of the third is the line x plus y equals six, which passes through the points zero, six and six, zero, and it is drawn solid because that symbol includes the line as well. The required region is the overlap of the three, and should be labelled R. To show that the point two, three lies inside it, substitute into all three inequalities. For the first, two is greater than or equal to one, which is true. For the second, three is greater than two, which is true. For the third, two plus three is five, which is less than or equal to six, so that is true as well. Since all three inequalities hold, the point lies inside the region.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The boundaries.**

- $x \geqslant 1$: the vertical line $x = 1$, **solid**, since the symbol includes the line.
- $y > x$: the line $y = x$, **dashed**, since the symbol is strict — points on it are **out**.
- $x + y \leqslant 6$: the line through $(0, 6)$ and $(6, 0)$, **solid**.

Shade the **overlap** of the three and label it **R**.

**Testing $(2, 3)$.**

- $x \geqslant 1$: $2 \geqslant 1$ ✓
- $y > x$: $3 > 2$ ✓
- $x + y \leqslant 6$: $2 + 3 = 5 \leqslant 6$ ✓

All three hold, so $(2, 3)$ is inside. Substituting into **every** inequality is what earns the final mark — checking one is not a demonstration.

questions.prompt: A student shades the region for $y > 2x - 1$ and includes the point $(1, 1)$, which lies on the boundary line. Explain the error, and describe a check that would have caught it.
questions.solution: The inequality is strictly greater than, so the boundary line itself is not part of the region and should be drawn dashed rather than solid. The point one, one lies exactly on the line, because two times one minus one is one, and the inequality requires y to be strictly greater than that value. Since one is not greater than one, the point does not satisfy the inequality and must be excluded from the region. The check that would have caught it is simply to substitute the point into the original inequality before including it. Putting x equal to one and y equal to one gives one is greater than one, which is false, so the point is not a solution. This is the two variable version of using an open circle on a number line, where the endpoint is excluded for a strict inequality.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The error.** $y > 2x - 1$ is **strict**, so the boundary is **not** part of the region and is drawn **dashed**.

**Why $(1, 1)$ is out.** It lies exactly **on** the line: $2(1) - 1 = 1$. The inequality needs $y$ **strictly greater** than that, and $1 > 1$ is **false**.

**The check.** Substitute the point into the original inequality before including it. $(1, 1)$ gives $1 > 1$ ✗ — caught in seconds.

This is the two-variable version of the **open circle** on a number line: a strict inequality always excludes its own boundary.

examTechnique.body:
Draw each boundary by treating the inequality as an equation, and use the **axis crossings** rather than a table of values.

Decide the line style before you draw it: dashed for a strict inequality, solid otherwise. It is a mark on its own.

Choose the side by substituting $(0, 0)$, or another point clearly off the line. Do not rearrange first.

Shade the overlap of all the inequalities, and **label it R**. If the question asks you to shade what fails instead, say so on the diagram.

Check by taking a point inside and testing it against every inequality, not just one.

If asked for a greatest or least value, test the corners only.

And remember a point on a dashed line is **not** in the region, however clearly it sits inside the shading.
examinerErrors: Drawing a solid line for a strict inequality, or a dashed line for an inclusive one.
Shading the wrong side, usually after rearranging and flipping a symbol.
Leaving the region unlabelled, so the diagram can be read either way.
Including a point that lies on a dashed boundary.
Making a table of values instead of using the axis crossings.
Checking only one inequality when confirming a point is inside.
Searching the interior for the largest value of an expression instead of testing the corners.
Shading the failing region when the question asked for the satisfying one, without saying which.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer decides each line style from the symbol before drawing anything, and picks the side by substituting rather than by reasoning, because it knows rearranging is where the flip happens. It labels R without being reminded, and states which convention it used when the question is ambiguous. Asked to justify that a point is inside, it substitutes into every inequality rather than the convenient one. And faced with a greatest-value question it goes straight to the corners, knowing that a linear expression cannot have an interior maximum.
